subtype: Approach: endless career quizzes and comparisons [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Yamini, and I shared a desk with Shalini the whole year we had to pick our Class 11 streams. I watched her disappear into career quizzes.

In June she did an aptitude test that said "Engineering". In July, another said "Creative Arts". She did a third to break the tie, and it said "Law". She laughed, then did five more. I saw her phone full of saved lists: "Top 50 careers for 2030", "20 jobs that will vanish", "Best careers for introverts".

Every Monday she'd tell me a new plan. By August she'd stopped telling me.

The form was due on 31 August. On the 30th, she sat on the steps outside the office with the blank form on her knee. She looked frozen.

I don't know what she was thinking. But when the peon locked the office door the next evening, her form was still blank.

qa.q: When was the stream form due?
What might Shalini have been feeling on the steps with the blank form?
qa.a: She probably felt frozen and overwhelmed, with too many conflicting results to choose from.

qa.q: What would have helped Shalini more than more quizzes?
qa.a: Picking two or three options, talking to a counsellor or people in those fields, and setting her own decision date before the deadline.

qa.q: How did Shalini's search look to Yamini?
qa.a: To Yamini it looked like a spiral of tests and lists ending in silence, though Yamini can't know exactly what she was thinking.

grounding: An observer describes a student taking many aptitude tests and reading many career lists, getting conflicting results and reaching the stream deadline without a decision.

Early March: Vandana took her first online aptitude test on a Sunday afternoon. Result: "Medicine". She told her brother Amandeep, excited. That night she took another. Result: "Journalism". She frowned and took a third.

Mid-April: Her laptop had twelve result screenshots and forty career-list tabs open. "Top careers for creative people." "Careers with the best pay." "Careers AI can't replace." Each one said something different. Amandeep asked what she'd chosen. "I need more data," she said, not looking up.

End of May: The school's stream selection form was due Friday. On Thursday night, Vandana sat on her bed surrounded by printouts, eyes red. "Every test says something else," she whispered. "I don't know what I am."

On Friday afternoon, Amandeep found the form still in her bag. The deadline had passed at noon. The school assigned her the stream with seats left.

qa.q: How many result screenshots did Vandana have by mid-April?
How did Vandana feel on Thursday night?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and lost, eyes red, saying she didn't know what she was.

qa.q: What would have been a better approach than more tests?
qa.a: Choosing a few options early, talking with a counsellor or people in those fields, and setting a personal decision date well before the deadline.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt finding the form still in her bag?
qa.a: Amandeep was probably upset and worried, having watched the search grow without any decision.

grounding: Shows a student taking many online aptitude tests and reading dozens of career lists, getting conflicting results and missing the stream deadline with no decision.
